paragraphs.heading: What it measures
paragraphs.text: The cumulative distribution function, or CDF, of a random variable X answers one question for any number x. What is the probability that X comes out at x or below? It is also called simply the distribution function of X. The same idea is used to describe random variables with several parts at once, known as multivariate ones.

paragraphs.heading: How it is written
paragraphs.text: A capital F usually names a CDF, while a lower-case f is kept for density and mass functions. When several random variables appear together, their letters are added as subscripts; with only one, the subscript is usually left off. Some well-known distributions have their own symbols. The normal distribution, for example, uses Φ and ϕ in place of F and f.

paragraphs.heading: Less than, or equal to
paragraphs.text: The "less than or equal to" in the definition is a convention, and not everyone follows it: Hungarian writing uses a strict less-than sign. The choice matters for discrete distributions. Reading tables of the binomial and Poisson distributions correctly depends on it. Paul Lévy's inversion formula for characteristic functions depends on the "or equal" version too.

paragraphs.heading: Its link to density
paragraphs.text: For a continuous distribution, the CDF equals the area under the probability density function, measured from negative infinity up to x. Going the other way, differentiating the CDF gives back the density, f(x) = dF(x)/dx, wherever that derivative exists. This step uses the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

paragraphs.heading: The upper tail
paragraphs.text: Sometimes the useful question is how often the variable lands above some level. That is the complementary CDF, also called the tail distribution. It is written F̄_X(x), and it equals 1 − F_X(x). In survival analysis it is called the survival function, S(x), and engineers call it the reliability function. When a test statistic has a continuous distribution, its one-sided p-value comes straight from this tail function.

paragraphs.heading: Running it backwards
paragraphs.text: If F is strictly increasing and continuous, each probability p between 0 and 1 matches exactly one number x with F(x) = p, written F⁻¹(p). This inverse is called the quantile function. It has a practical use. Take a variable Y spread uniformly over the interval from 0 to 1 and feed it into F⁻¹, and the result is distributed as F, which is how inverse transform sampling generates random numbers.

paragraphs.heading: Estimating it from data
paragraphs.text: The empirical distribution function is an estimate of the CDF, built from the points in a sample. It converges, with probability 1, to the underlying distribution that produced those points. A number of results measure how fast that convergence happens.
